entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Blount County, Alabama (1850–1870)

## Jurisdiction
Blount County formed 1818, county seat Oneonta. Boundaries stable 1850–1870. Standard place: Blount, Alabama, United States.

## Census records
- **1850 federal** (pop.): NARA M432 Roll 2 — 99% indexed, FamilySearch (imageGroup 004187292)
- **1855 Alabama State Census**: Collection 1915984, indexed, FamilySearch
- **1860 federal** (pop.): NARA M653 Roll 2 (Bibb & Blount) — 99% indexed, FamilySearch (imageGroup 005154190)
- **1866 Alabama State Census**: Collection 1915987, 243K records, indexed, FamilySearch
- **1870 federal** (pop.): NARA M593 Roll 3 — 96% indexed, FamilySearch (imageGroup 004257477)

## Vital records
Alabama civil registration began 1908. Pre-1908 births/deaths found in church records, cemetery inscriptions, probate files, family bibles.

## Marriage records
FamilySearch has Blount County marriage registers indexed at 83–85%:
- 1820–1860 (vols. A–B): imageGroup 007316661
- 1860–1871: imageGroup 007316662
- 1868–1888: imageGroup 007316663
Religious Marriage Parental Consent Records 1852–1866 (100% indexed; name parents): imageGroups 004484211_003/004
Also: Alabama County Marriages 1711–1992 (collection 1743384).

## Probate records
Digitized on FamilySearch, mostly full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed (0% recordSearchablePercent). Use full-text search.
- 1845–1869: multiple volumes
- Estate Files 1830–1976: collection 1978117 (25K records)
- Probate Records 1809–1985: collection 1925446 (browse-only)

## Land/Deed records
All browse-only or full-text only (0% name-indexed) on FamilySearch:
- 1840–1871: imageGroups 008486312/313/314
- BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov) for federal land patents

## Church records
- Alabama Church Records 1831–1994: collection 2790182
- Blount County church volumes 1820–1901: imageGroup 008182846 (full-text)
- Parish Records 1832–1920: imageGroup 008493197 (browse-only)
Dominating denominations: Baptist, Methodist

## Military
- Confederate service: collection 1932139 (1.2M indexed)
- Union service: collection 1932389 (31K indexed)

## Cemetery
- Tombstone inscriptions 1814–1975 + obituaries: imageGroup 007492923 (full-text)
- FindAGrave; ALGenWeb Tombstone Transcription Project

## Key tips
1. No civil birth/death records before 1908.
2. The 1860 census (99% indexed) is the primary tool for the M M Wood household.
3. Parental Consent Records (100% indexed) name parents of brides/grooms.
4. Martha Wood born in Georgia ~1855 — search northern Georgia 1850 census in parallel.
5. Use FamilySearch full-text search for deed, probate, court volumes.

entry.rationale: The 1860 U.S. Census for Blount County is the primary direct source for identifying Martha J. Wood's parents. Source Q3ZW-YBN in tree.gedcomx.json is an index entry pointing to an 'M M Wood / Martha Wood' household in Blount County, but it has not been formally extracted into this project. The full census image (NARA M653 Roll 2, 99% name-indexed on FamilySearch, imageGroup 005154190) will name all household members with ages, relationships, and birthplaces — directly identifying M M Wood's full name, wife's name and age, and confirming Martha's presence as a child. This is foundational for all subsequent searches.

Martha J. Wood married W. F. Lanham in Hill County, Texas on 7 Jan 1869 (source WWLY-J9X in tree.gedcomx.json). At ~age 14, Texas law required parental consent for her marriage. The original marriage record image — and any associated consent bond or license — may directly name her parents (father's name and signature on the consent). This is potentially the highest-yield record for the parentage question and should be examined alongside the 1860 census. Collection: Texas, County Marriage Records, 1837-2010 on FamilySearch.

Martha J. Wood was born circa 1855 in Georgia, so her parents were in Georgia before migrating to Alabama. The 1850 U.S. Census (taken before Martha's birth) will show M M Wood's household in Georgia: his full name, wife's name and maiden name (if recently married), older children, ages, and birthplaces — establishing the family's Georgia county of origin. This is essential for identifying Martha's mother and the family's geographic roots. The 1850 census is heavily indexed on FamilySearch nationally. The specific Georgia county is unknown until the 1860 census extract provides birthplace data; search Georgia statewide for 'Wood' households matching the profile.

Dedicated search for the marriage of M M Wood in Blount County, Alabama. Per the record-type guide, a parentage plan must include a separate item for the parents' marriage: (a) it confirms M M Wood and his wife as a couple; (b) it supplies Martha's mother's maiden name, which census records omit; (c) its date relative to Martha's ~1855 birth corroborates the spousal unit. Blount County marriage registers 1820-1860 and 1860-1871 are 84-85% indexed on FamilySearch (collections 1743384 and 1674672; imageGroups 007316661/007316662). Also search the Religious Marriage Parental Consent Records 1852-1860 (100% indexed, imageGroup 004484211_003) which name parents of brides and grooms.

Fallback for pli_004: if M M Wood married in Georgia before migrating to Alabama (likely, given Martha's Georgia birth ~1855), his marriage record will be in Georgia county records. Georgia County Marriages, 1785-1950 (collection 1927197, 1.9M records) and Georgia Marriages, 1808-1967 (collection 1674807, 663K records) are indexed on FamilySearch. This record will name his wife's maiden name — Martha's maternal grandmother's maiden name — and the Georgia county of marriage, directing the 1850 census search to a specific county.

The 1855 Alabama State Census (collection 1915984, 34,978 records, indexed on FamilySearch) provides a mid-decade check between 1850 and 1860. If the Wood family had already migrated from Georgia to Alabama by 1855, this census would confirm their presence in Blount County, show household members including any children born before Martha, and narrow the migration window. If the family does not appear, the migration window tightens to 1855-1860. Lower priority than the 1860 federal census but useful corroboration.

entry.narrative_markdown:
# Parents of Martha J. Wood (LKYG-VKB)

## Conclusion (Probable)

The preponderance of evidence strongly suggests that **M M Wood** (tree person I1, born approximately 1812 in South Carolina) and **Martha Wood** (tree person I2, born approximately 1814 in South Carolina) are the parents of Martha J. Wood (tree person LKYG-VKB; born approximately 1852–1855 in Georgia; died 30 May 1906, Hill County, Texas), the mother of Jimmie Jewel Neal. Three independent US Federal Census enumerations spanning 1850–1870 document the same family unit in a consistent pattern that supports this conclusion, though the parentage rests on indirect evidence (household co-residence) rather than a direct statement.

## Primary Evidence

The 1860 United States Census for Blount County, Alabama, places a child named "Martha Wood" — female, born approximately 1852 in Georgia — in the household of head "M M Wood" and wife "Martha Wood," both born in South Carolina.\textsuperscript{1} M M Wood is enumerated as approximately 48 years old (born approximately 1812) and his wife as approximately 46 years old (born approximately 1814). The child Martha Wood (approximately age 8, born approximately 1852 in Georgia) matches tree person LKYG-VKB in sex, approximate birth year, birthplace (Georgia), and 1860 residence (Blount County, Alabama). Because the 1860 Federal Census did not include a relationship column, the parent-child relationship is inferred from household position and shared surname — a method that constitutes indirect evidence. The record was accessed as a derivative FamilySearch index entry for the underlying NARA microfilm schedule (M653); the original image was not independently examined.

## Corroborating Evidence

**1850 Cherokee County, Georgia census.** A search of the 1850 US Federal Census found a household of "M M Wood" in Cherokee County, Georgia: head M M Wood, male, approximately 34 years old (born approximately 1816), birthplace South Carolina; wife "Martha Wood," female, approximately 27 years old (born approximately 1823), birthplace South Carolina; and seven children born between approximately 1837 and 1849, in South Carolina and Georgia.\textsuperscript{2} Three of these children — Margaret (born approximately 1841, Georgia), Manly A (born approximately 1843, Georgia), and David (born approximately 1844, Georgia) — appear age-consistently in both the 1850 Cherokee County household and a 1860 Blount County household containing identically-named adults, confirming these as the same family unit. Martha J. Wood had not yet been born at the time of the 1850 census, consistent with her absence from that household.

**1870 Blount County, Alabama census.** A household headed by "J T Wood" — male, approximately 58 years old (born approximately 1812), birthplace South Carolina — was found in Blount County, Alabama, in 1870.\textsuperscript{3} His wife is recorded as "M Wood," female, approximately 55 years old (born approximately 1815), birthplace South Carolina. Two Georgia-born adult children remain in the household: Jasper Wood (male, born approximately 1848, Georgia) and Elizabeth Wood (female, born approximately 1852, Georgia). The head's given-name initials differ from the 1860 census ("J T" versus "M M"), but all other identifying attributes agree: identical birth year (~1812), identical birth state (South Carolina), same county (Blount, Alabama), same wife (Martha/M Wood, born South Carolina approximately 1814–1815), and Georgia-born children consistent with the 1850 family. This discrepancy is attributed to different enumerators recording different initials for the same individual. This 1870 record is linked to I1 and I2 at probable confidence.

## Evidence Analysis

**Source classification.** All three census records were accessed as derivative FamilySearch index entries pointing to original NARA population schedules. The underlying federal census schedules are original government records. The original census images were not independently examined in this research project, which is a noted limitation. For the parentage question, household composition — which the FamilySearch census indexes capture reliably — is the critical evidence type.

**Informant analysis.** The informants in all three censuses were unidentified household members who responded to the enumerator's questions. Ages and birthplaces are secondary information (reported from memory, not from contemporaneous documentation). Household co-residence is primary information (the enumerator observed it directly at enumeration time). The parentage inference is indirect: in the 1860 census, without a relationship column, parentage is inferred from the surname, sex, approximate age, birthplace, and household position of child_7 Martha Wood relative to head M M Wood and wife Martha Wood.

**Independence.** The three census enumerations are mutually independent: conducted by different enumerators in different years (1850, 1860, 1870), one in Georgia (1850) and two in Alabama (1860, 1870). They constitute three separate evidentiary units.

## Conflicts Resolved

**c_001 — M M Wood birth year (~1812 vs. ~1816).** The 1860 and 1870 censuses agree on a birth year of approximately 1812 (assertions a_086, a_004); the 1850 census gives approximately 1816 (assertion a_028). The two-to-one preponderance favors ~1812. A 4-year discrepancy across pre-1880 censuses is within the documented range of census age-estimation error. Preferred assertion: a_086.

**c_002 — Martha Wood birth year (~1814 vs. ~1815 vs. ~1823).** The 1860 census gives approximately 1814 (a_092) and the 1870 census gives approximately 1815 (a_009), agreeing within 1 year; the 1850 census gives approximately 1823 (a_033), a 9-year outlier. The two-to-one preponderance favors ~1814. The 1850 outlier is consistent with the documented historical pattern of women in the antebellum South understating their ages to census enumerators. Preferred assertion: a_092.

A discrepancy in Martha J. Wood's birth year — approximately 1855 in the pre-existing tree versus approximately 1852 in the 1860 census index — is noted but does not constitute a separate source conflict (both values ultimately reference the same 1860 census source S3). This does not affect the parentage conclusion.

## Limitations and Path to Proof

This conclusion is rated **probable** rather than proved because: (1) all three sources are derivative indexes, and the original NARA census images were not independently examined; (2) the parentage rests on indirect evidence from household co-residence in a census without a relationship column; and (3) no source with direct, primary parentage information was found.

The tier could potentially be advanced if the following records — currently unsearched or inaccessible — were found: a probate estate file naming Martha J. Wood as a daughter of M M Wood (Blount County, Alabama estate records for 1870–1900 are not yet accessible via FamilySearch full-text search); a marriage record for M M Wood that would name his wife's maiden surname (likely in South Carolina approximately 1835–1837, in records not yet indexed on FamilySearch); or a later census with an explicit relationship column (e.g., the 1880 US Census) showing Martha's parents, if any of the family remained together.

# Parents of Martha J. Wood (LKYG-VKB)

## Conclusion (Probable)

The preponderance of evidence strongly suggests that **M M Wood** (tree person I1, born approximately 1812 in South Carolina) and **Martha Wood** (tree person I2, born approximately 1814 in South Carolina) are the parents of Martha J. Wood (tree person LKYG-VKB; born approximately 1852–1855 in Georgia; died 30 May 1906, Hill County, Texas), the mother of Jimmie Jewel Neal. Three independent US Federal Census enumerations spanning 1850–1870 document the same family unit in a consistent pattern that supports this conclusion, though the parentage rests on indirect evidence (household co-residence) rather than a direct statement.

## Primary Evidence

The 1860 United States Census for Blount County, Alabama, places a child named "Martha Wood" — female, born approximately 1852 in Georgia — in the household of head "M M Wood" and wife "Martha Wood," both born in South Carolina.\textsuperscript{1} M M Wood is enumerated as approximately 48 years old (born approximately 1812) and his wife as approximately 46 years old (born approximately 1814). The child Martha Wood (approximately age 8, born approximately 1852 in Georgia) matches tree person LKYG-VKB in sex, approximate birth year, birthplace (Georgia), and 1860 residence (Blount County, Alabama). Because the 1860 Federal Census did not include a relationship column, the parent-child relationship is inferred from household position and shared surname — a method that constitutes indirect evidence. The record was accessed as a derivative FamilySearch index entry for the underlying NARA microfilm schedule (M653); the original image was not independently examined.

The search that returned this record (log_001) produced four candidates in Blount County, Alabama. The top-scored result was "Martha Ann Wood" (ark MHDC-PPS, score 6.9236), born 1857 in **Alabama**, in the household of "H W Wood" — a different head of household. This competing candidate was considered and ruled out (h_001): tree person LKYG-VKB is documented as born in Georgia (assertion a_135, and the pre-existing tree birth fact), while MHDC-PPS records the child as Alabama-born. A child born in Alabama cannot be the same person as one born in Georgia when both birthplaces come from the same contemporaneous census enumeration. The accepted record (MHDC-LKY, score 6.9136, in M M Wood's household) is preferred on this unambiguous birthplace criterion.

## Corroborating Evidence

**1850 Cherokee County, Georgia census.** A search of the 1850 US Federal Census found a household of "M M Wood" in Cherokee County, Georgia: head M M Wood, male, approximately 34 years old (born approximately 1816), birthplace South Carolina; wife "Martha Wood," female, approximately 27 years old (born approximately 1823), birthplace South Carolina; and seven children born between approximately 1837 and 1849, in South Carolina and Georgia.\textsuperscript{2} Two of these children — Manly A (born approximately 1843, Georgia) and David (born approximately 1844, Georgia) — appear age-consistently in both the 1850 Cherokee County household and the 1860 Blount County household, confirming these as the same family unit. Martha J. Wood had not yet been born at the time of the 1850 census, consistent with her absence from that household. (Note: Margaret, listed in both households, is recorded as born in Georgia in the 1850 census but in South Carolina in the 1860 census — a minor discrepancy in one child’s birthplace that does not undermine the identification given the agreement on Manly A and David as cross-census anchors.)

**1870 Blount County, Alabama census.** A household headed by "J T Wood" — male, approximately 58 years old (born approximately 1812), birthplace South Carolina — was found in Blount County, Alabama, in 1870.\textsuperscript{3} His wife is recorded as "M Wood," female, approximately 55 years old (born approximately 1815), birthplace South Carolina. Two Georgia-born adult children remain in the household: Jasper Wood (male, born approximately 1848, Georgia) and Elizabeth Wood (female, born approximately 1852, Georgia). The head's given-name initials differ from the 1860 census ("J T" versus "M M"), but all other identifying attributes agree: identical birth year (~1812), identical birth state (South Carolina), same county (Blount, Alabama), same wife (Martha/M Wood, born South Carolina approximately 1814–1815), and Georgia-born children consistent with the 1850 family. This discrepancy is attributed to different enumerators recording different initials for the same individual. This 1870 record is linked to I1 and I2 at probable confidence.

## Evidence Analysis

**Source classification.** All three census records were accessed as derivative FamilySearch index entries pointing to original NARA population schedules. The underlying federal census schedules are original government records. The original census images were not independently examined in this research project, which is a noted limitation. For the parentage question, household composition — which the FamilySearch census indexes capture reliably — is the critical evidence type.

**Informant analysis.** The informants in all three censuses were unidentified household members who responded to the enumerator's questions. Ages and birthplaces are secondary information (reported from memory, not from contemporaneous documentation). Household co-residence is primary information (the enumerator observed it directly at enumeration time). The parentage inference is indirect: in the 1860 census, without a relationship column, parentage is inferred from the surname, sex, approximate age, birthplace, and household position of child_7 Martha Wood relative to head M M Wood and wife Martha Wood.

**Independence.** The three census enumerations are mutually independent: conducted by different enumerators in different years (1850, 1860, 1870), one in Georgia (1850) and two in Alabama (1860, 1870). They constitute three separate evidentiary units.

## Conflicts Resolved

**c_001 — M M Wood birth year (~1812 vs. ~1816).** The 1860 and 1870 censuses agree on a birth year of approximately 1812 (assertions a_086, a_004); the 1850 census gives approximately 1816 (assertion a_028). The two-to-one preponderance favors ~1812. A 4-year discrepancy across pre-1880 censuses is within the documented range of census age-estimation error. Preferred assertion: a_086.

**c_002 — Martha Wood birth year (~1814 vs. ~1815 vs. ~1823).** The 1860 census gives approximately 1814 (a_092) and the 1870 census gives approximately 1815 (a_009), agreeing within 1 year; the 1850 census gives approximately 1823 (a_033), a 9-year outlier. The two-to-one preponderance favors ~1814. The 1850 outlier is consistent with the documented historical pattern of women in the antebellum South understating their ages to census enumerators. Preferred assertion: a_092.

A discrepancy in Martha J. Wood’s birth year — approximately 1855 in the pre-existing tree versus approximately 1852 in the 1860 census index — is noted but does not constitute a separate source conflict (both values ultimately reference the same 1860 census source S3). This does not affect the parentage conclusion.

## Limitations and Path to Proof

This conclusion is rated **probable** rather than proved because: (1) all three sources are derivative indexes, and the original NARA census images were not independently examined; (2) the parentage rests on indirect evidence from household co-residence in a census without a relationship column; and (3) no source with direct, primary parentage information was found.

The tier could potentially be advanced if the following records — currently unsearched or inaccessible — were found: a probate estate file naming Martha J. Wood as a daughter of M M Wood (Blount County, Alabama estate records for 1870–1900 are not yet accessible via FamilySearch full-text search); a marriage record for M M Wood that would name his wife’s maiden surname (likely in South Carolina approximately 1835–1837, in records not yet indexed on FamilySearch); or a later census with an explicit relationship column (e.g., the 1880 US Census) showing Martha’s parents, if any of the family remained together.
